e.etymology: A modern American name that joins the Ky- of Kyle and Kylan to the -land ending of Ryland and Leland.
For boys, the form of John used in Dutch, Czech, Polish and the Scandinavian languages, from Latin Johannes and Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. For girls, an English short form of Janet or Janice.
namesakes: Jan Brady (the middle sister on The Brady Bunch)
e.note: Americans tend to read Jan as a woman's name said JAN; the European boys' name is said YAHN.

e.etymology: Of mixed origin: perhaps from Selma, a place in Macpherson's Ossian poems, or a short form of Anselma. In Turkish and Bosnian use it comes from Arabic Salma, safe.
namesakes: Selma Blair (actress in Cruel Intentions and Legally Blonde)
Selma Bouvier (Marge's sister on The Simpsons)
Selma Lagerlöf (Swedish novelist, first woman to win the Nobel in Literature)

assoc.t: Selma, Alabama, site of the 1965 voting rights marches
Selma, the 2014 film about Martin Luther King Jr.

e.etymology: From Bricius, the Latin name of a 5th-century bishop of Tours, probably from a Gaulish word meaning speckled. Brice is the French and older English spelling; Bryce is now more common in the US.
The French and Portuguese form of Alexander, from Greek Alexandros, built from alexein, to defend, and aner, man. Alexander the Great spread the name across Europe and Asia.
namesakes: Alexandre Dumas (French author of The Three Musketeers)

e.etymology: A modern American spelling alongside Kia and Kiah, close in sound to Kiana and Kiara. Kiya was also the name of a wife of the Egyptian pharaoh Akhenaten.

assoc.t: Kia, the Korean car maker, sounds the same

e.etymology: A variant of Uriah, from Hebrew Uriyah, the Lord is my light. Uriah the Hittite was Bathsheba's soldier husband; Urijah is the King James spelling for several lesser biblical figures.
namesakes: Urijah Faber (UFC Hall of Fame fighter)

e.etymology: An American elaboration from the 1990s that builds on Rome, Romeo and Romell with the Italian-style -ello ending.
An American name in the family of Zariyah, Jaliyah and Mariyah, joining the Ja- beginning to the -riyah ending. It also matches Arabic jariyah, flowing, as in sadaqah jariyah, ongoing charity.
e.note: In Arabic jariyah means flowing but is also the classical word for a slave girl, which Arabic speakers may notice.

e.etymology: From Hindi neev, the foundation of a building, used as a modern boys' name in India. It is unrelated to the Irish girls' name Niamh, which is sometimes spelled Neve.
A doubled-a spelling of Ayla, a Turkish name for the halo of light around the moon, from ay, moon; Ayla is also a Hebrew name meaning oak. Star Wars fans know the Jedi Aayla Secura.

assoc.t: Aayla Secura, a blue-skinned Jedi in Star Wars

e.etymology: A modern American name that blends Avery with the -ly ending of Everly and Beverly.
A modern American compound of the word name River and the -lyn ending of Evelyn and Brooklyn.
A spelling of Devin and Devon. Devin is an Irish surname related to Devine, and Devon is the English county; in Indian families Devan is a separate name from Sanskrit deva, god.
A respelling of Joy, the English word taken up as a name by Puritans in the 17th century. The word comes through Old French joie from Latin gaudia.

assoc.t: Joi, the holographic companion in Blade Runner 2049

e.note: In capitals, JOI is a common internet abbreviation for a genre of adult video.

e.etymology: From Hebrew barukh, blessed, the opening word of Jewish blessings. In the Bible Baruch is the scribe and companion of the prophet Jeremiah.

assoc.t: Baruch College of the City University of New York

e.etymology: A modern American name built from Ireland with the -lynn ending, in use alongside Irelyn and Ireland itself.
In Argentina and Chile, Ailén is a Mapuche name from aylen, ember. The same spelling also turns up as a variant of Aileen, the Scottish form of Eileen.
e.note: Easily misread or autocorrected as the word alien.

e.etymology: From Spanish dolores, sorrows, shortened from María de los Dolores, a title of the Virgin Mary as Our Lady of Sorrows. English speakers borrowed it in the 19th century.
namesakes: Dolores Huerta (labor leader, co-founder of the United Farm Workers)
Dolores Umbridge (villain of the Harry Potter series)
Dolores O'Riordan (lead singer of The Cranberries)

assoc.t: Dolores, the cousin who hears everything in Encanto

e.etymology: The everyday short form of David, from Hebrew Dawid, beloved, sometimes given as a name in its own right.
namesakes: Dave Grohl (Foo Fighters frontman and Nirvana drummer)
Dave Matthews (leader of the Dave Matthews Band)

assoc.t: Dave, a mobile banking and cash-advance app
Dave & Buster's, restaurant and arcade chain

e.etymology: A variant of DeShawn, an African American name that adds the prefix De- or Da- to Shawn, the Anglicized spelling of Irish Seán (John).
In the US mostly a Spanish-language spelling of Mayra, a name of uncertain source. In Brazil Maíra comes from Old Tupi, and in Latvia Maira is a form of Marija (Mary).
A spelling of Madeline, the English form of French Madeleine, from Mary Magdalene's title, of Magdala, a village on the Sea of Galilee whose name means tower.
Maria spelled backwards, a way of reworking a family name that is popular in Latino families. In the Canary Islands Airam is also a boys' name credited to the indigenous Guanche people.
A pet form of Alfred, from Old English Ælfræd, elf counsel, now given as a name in its own right. It has ranked among the most popular boys' names in England since the 2000s.
namesakes: Alfie Allen (Theon Greyjoy on Game of Thrones)

assoc.t: Alfie, the London womanizer of the 1966 and 2004 films

e.etymology: A short form of names beginning with Aur-, such as Aurora (dawn) and Aurelia (golden), now used on its own. In Finland Auri is a variant of Aura; fantasy readers know Auri from Patrick Rothfuss's novels.

assoc.t: Auri in Patrick Rothfuss's Kingkiller Chronicle

e.etymology: A respelling of Amira, the feminine of Arabic amir, prince or commander.
A spelling of Remy, the French form of Latin Remigius, from remex, oarsman. St Remigius baptized the Frankish king Clovis around 500.

assoc.t: Remy, the rat chef in Pixar's Ratatouille (same sound)

e.etymology: An English and Scottish occupational surname for a standard-bearer, from the word banner, which came through Old French baniere. It also reads as the ordinary word for a flag.

assoc.t: Bruce Banner, the Hulk's alter ego in Marvel stories
banner, the ordinary word for a flag or a web ad

e.etymology: The English word lively, full of life and energy, which is also a surname that began as a nickname. Most Americans know the surname from actress Blake Lively.

assoc.t: Blake Lively, the Gossip Girl actress

e.etymology: A South Asian name also written Aira and Ayra. Name lists call it Arabic and gloss it as noble or respected, but no clear Arabic source is established.
A pet form of Katherine and Kathleen that became a given name in its own right in the mid-20th century. Katherine comes from Greek Aikaterine, long linked with katharos, pure.
namesakes: Kathy Hochul (New York's first female governor)
